newsitem.title: USA: US economy performing extraordinarily well - Parry. [CORRECTED 09:00 GMT 9/8]
newsitem.headline: US economy performing extraordinarily well - Parry. [CORRECTED 09:00 GMT 9/8]

text.p: The U.S. economy has performed extraordinarily well, as evidenced by strong second quarter growth and the lowest unemployment rates in 24 years, San Francisco Federal Reserve Bank President Robert Parry said.
"The national economy has been performing extraordinarily well," Parry said in a prepared speech to the Northwest Taxable Bond Club in Bellevue, Washington on Friday.
He said the 3.3 percent real GDP growth between Q2 1996 and Q2 1997 was all the more impressive given that the economy is in the seventh year of its expansion.
(Corrects to clarify reference to 3.3 percent growth rate)
But while the economy is running at full tide, Parry also questioned whether those conditions would last.
"Like any economist, I'm also a little suspicious of claims that the tide is sweeping us to some brave new world...where inflation is dead and where the good times roll on forever," Parry said.

Parry said the low-inflation environment as evidenced by a 2-1/2 percent increase in the core Consumer Price Index this year may be a result of several factors: a recent deceleration in employers' benefits costs; an increase in the value of the dollar; and a possible productivity surge.

The rising dollar is helping to hold down the price of many imports, he said, but it is not a permanent fix against inflation pressures. Of the three factors, Parry said rising productivity is most likely to have a long-term effect.
Parry expected the nearly 24 percent rise in high-tech investment last year to payoff in terms of productivity.
"It's certainly likely that productivity is being boosted by the technological advances associated with computers and other high-tech developments," he said.
Parry stressed that the factors behind the economy's ability to post high-speed growth and high resource utilization without igniting inflation do not support a claim that inflation is dead.
The chances of higher inflation in the future could be curbed by a slowing of the economy to a more sustainable growth rate he said, adding that this was happening now.
A more sustainable growth rate should be expected based on a strong dollar, a "breather" in strong spending for "real assets" and restrained federal spending, Parry said.
Finally, Parry said, the Fed remains committed to its goal in delivering maximum sustainable growth for the economy by keeping inflationary pressures under control.
"We're prepared to act to head off any inflationary threat that may arise," he said.
